chunks: What a 10x probe attenuator does. The question: What does the 10x attenuation do on a probe?
A 10x probe has a 9 megohms resistor in its tip. With the scope's 1 megohms input it forms a voltage divider, so the scope sees one tenth of the signal.
You tell the scope the probe is 10x, so it multiplies the display by ten and you read the real voltage. The main benefit is that the circuit sees a much lighter load.
A map drawn at one-tenth scale shrinks everything by ten, and you multiply by ten to get the real distance. The probe shrinks the signal by ten and the scope multiplies it back.
One subtlety the map hides: the divider must shrink fast and slow signals equally, which a small capacitor in the tip ensures.
The top block (R 1 with C 1) and the bottom block (R 2 with C 2) are each a resistor with a capacitor in parallel.
Each has the same time constant when R 1C 1 = R 2C 2, so each behaves as the same fraction at every frequency, and the ratio is 1:10 at all frequencies.
Voltage divider: two resistors that split a voltage in proportion to their sizes. Capacitance: stored-charge behavior that loads fast signals (pF = trillionth of a farad).
Less is better. Compensation: adjusting a small trimmer capacitor in the probe so the 10:1 ratio holds at all speeds.
Probe attenuation setting: the scope's 1x or 10x entry that rescales the display.
Probe a 5 volts signal. The 9 megohms and 1 megohms divide it by ten, so 0. 5 volts reaches the scope's input. With the scope set to 10x, it shows 5 volts.
A bare cable (a 1x probe) would put about 1 megohms and 100 picofarads on the circuit.
At 10 megahertz, 100 picofarads acts like 1 over (2 pi times 10 to the 7 times 10 to the -10) about 160 ohms , a heavy load.
The 10x probe shows about 10 megohms and 10 picofarads, which at 10 megahertz is about 1. 6 kilohms. To check compensation, probe the scope's square-wave test output.
A flat top is right; rounded corners or overshoot mean adjust the trimmer. That is the whole idea.

"The 10x probe is a built-in voltage divider: 9 megaohms in the tip and the scope's 1 megaohm give a 10:1 reduction, so the circuit sees about 10 megaohms and roughly 10 picofarads instead of 1 megaohm and about 100 picofarads.
A trimmer capacitor across the 9 megaohm resistor equalizes the time constants, R 1C 1 equals R 2C 2 , so the ratio stays 10:1 at all frequencies.
I adjust it with the square-wave output. The cost is ten times less signal, so noise matters more."
